# C++ Refactoring Implementation and Documentation

[C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%2B%2B) (CPP) is a programming language cited as high-level for general-purpose programming. Because of this inherent depth, many with creative or even logistical reasoning that don’t know the built-in syntax of CPP can’t operate as well as those who utilize this high-level language. To address the challenges of complex programming, Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) employs a visual scripting language called [Blueprints](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/blueprints-visual-scripting-in-unreal-engine) (BP). This tool was specifically designed to provide a simpler alternative to in-depth programming. BP consists of nodes and object-oriented classes, making them highly flexible for use by designers who are familiar with visual scripting. Vespa Mode knew eventually they’d refactor towards CPP but didn’t realize the portion for which needed to be refactored. The refactoring targeted critical performance bottlenecks while maintaining the project’s architectural integrity and visual quality systems. The implementation and optimization will be categorized via pro et contra, and an experiment will be conducted with the refactored portion of the Vespa Mode Project comparing such to the unrefactored portion.

# Blueprint (BP) Implementation Analysis

  (ADV)  ***i.***	    The advantages of BP Implementation in Vespa Mode 

| ![][image1] |
| ----- |
| Figure 1: “[Images of the two BP functions used in Vespa Mode](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zxTX6ddHFm2LKKM1YiG4t7UcXhRvJgAL/view?usp=sharing)” |

The implementation of BP utilized rapid prototyping, where the simplicity of the interface granted fast development of features in the initial project phase despite the very limited time constraints. The beginner-friendly visual interface provided an easily accessible entry point for team members who had limited UE5 experience. UE5’s unique [macros](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/macros-in-unreal-engine) accessible within the CPP framework allowed the team to reference and use CPP functions inside of [Event Graphs](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/event-graph-in-unreal-engine); these functions were planned out to be implemented in the future and replaced their BP equivalents. Editor integration allowed real-time changes without compilation to facilitate iterative design. Each component in this engine is clearly separated, backed by an individual [Event Graph](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/event-graph-in-unreal-engine) enhancing organization. The clarity of simple logic in BP is quite straightforward, visually representing basic game logic.

(DISADV)  ***ii.***	    The disadvantages of BP Implementation in Vespa Mode

| ![][image2] |
| ----- |
| Figure 2: “[Images of the two BP functions used in Vespa Mode](https://drive.google.com/file/d/109aZmzwg6E_bxeyeVsTotSgk4IL9HIkf/view?usp=sharing)” |

The implementation of BP gave visual complexity, as complex logic now became difficult to parse visually as the function size increased. There were performance concerns, as there was significant performance overhead compared to native CPP, which was problematic for frequently called functions. There were tick-based performance issues, as the two major functions operating on [Event Tick](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/BlueprintAPI/AddEvent/EventTick) created scaling performance bottlenecks. The maintenance challenges from large BP networks which  became harder to debug and modify overtime.

(IMP)  ***iii.***	    The implications going forward in Vespa Mode optimization

The BP allowed for fast prototyping, but by the time it came to scaling the project, BP became really bad, especially for the issue of performance as it relates to tick-based performance bottlenecks. This means going forward, Vespa Mode now realizes the utility of BP and now can utilize a hybrid that addresses the concerns of performance via CPP but uses the majority of the simplicity systems with BP.

# CPP Refactoring Rationale

 ***i.***	    The Targeted Refactoring Scope: Throttle Control Function 

| ![][image3] |
| ----- |
| Figure 3: ‘[Images of CPP Refactoring used in Vespa Mode](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1yjeFoRS9whqkNVhAAS0WbbLjjznfKfdz/view?usp=sharing)’ |

The refactoring of CPP focused specifically on two critical functions that presented performance challenges. There was the throttle control function and the turning control function. The throttle control function handles continuous vehicle acceleration input. You can see Figure 3 attached gives the throttle control function. 

 ***ii.***	    The Targeted Refactoring Scope: Turning Control Function 

| ![][image4] |
| ----- |
| Figure 4: ‘[Images of CPP Refactoring used in Vespa Mode](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1G4GiS_FLscg6j4Jodd9UqX_jn1Mcp695/view?usp=sharing)’ |

The refactoring of CPP focused specifically on two critical functions that presented performance challenges. There was the throttle control function and the turning control function. The turning control function manages real-time steering mechanics. You can see Figure 4 attached gives the throttle control function. 

 ***iii.***	    Why These Functions Were Chosen

These functions were chosen due to the frequency of execution, both functions operated on Event Tick (executing every frame). There was a performance impact as the cumulative overhead of BP execution every frame created measure performance degradation. The scalability concerns occurred as the project grew in complexity which these functions became the primary bottlenecks and the readability as the complex logic was actually clearer in CPP code than in large Blueprint networks. 

# Technical Implementation Process

 ***i.***	    Visual Studio Integration // BP to CPP

The development environmental setup gave us Visual Studio Integration, which configured Visual Studio with Unreal Engine development tools. The project conversion consisted of creating a CPP class in the editor to convert the project to a CPP project type. The class inheritance structure parented existing BP classes to new CPP base classes.

 ***ii.***	    Code Integration Strategy

| ![][image5] |
| ----- |
| Figure 5: ‘[Images of CPP Refactoring used in Vespa Mode](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MR80q72AS3XI-dEhNeQE_NIdbdTV4ZcY/view?usp=sharing)’ |

The Vespa Mode integration strategy consisted of employing Unreal Engine [macros](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/macros-in-unreal-engine) ([UFUNCTION](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/API/Runtime/CoreUObject/UFunction/__ctor?application_version=5.7), [UPROPERTY](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/API/Runtime/CoreUObject/UProperty?application_version=5.7)) to maintain BP accessibility. Parameter pinning configured functions to accept input via BP node pins, preserving existing component connections. Incremental migration, which maintained functional BP implementation while CPP versions were developed and tested.

(ADV)  ***iii.***	    Results and Performance Metrics

There were significant performance improvements from the refactoring and optimization techniques used during Vespa Mode. An example of an optimization technique used would be notably the water systems as documented [here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1DCFiaAqEIbCvxEztRlQeoQXzop8-dCwC/view?usp=sharing), but there is now reduced CPU overhead, which is a significant reduction in per-frame processing time; improved scalability, as better performance under increased object counts and complexity; and maintained visual quality, as all visual optimization techniques were preserved during refactoring. There were long-term benefits such as improved code maintainability and performance headroom, and now there is hybrid approach viability as demonstrated by the effective combination of BP for design and CPP for performance-critical systems.

(DISADV)  ***iv.***	    Developmental Impact

The initial setup challenges included a two-week period of configuration issues and project corruption resolution. The implementation was slower because of the lack of connection to the editor and the existing safety protocols. Additionally, the unfamiliarity with the engine-specific setup resulted in minimal progress.

# Performance Testing Methodology & Results

Experiment Overview:

To objectively compare BP vs CPP performance in Vespa mode, we experimented with a test that isolates the execution time of identical logic with both systems.

 ***i.***	    Testing Procedure: Timing Mechanism

| ![][image6] |
| ----- |
| Figure 6: ‘[Images of Test Functions](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1v5VKCzn7El6eQ4nbDX1MthCja-P8PvPG/view?usp=sharing)’ |

We used the [Now()](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/BlueprintAPI/Math/DateTime/Now) function to capture precise timestamps before and after function execution. The Start Time is recorded immediately before function call and the End Time is recorded immediately after function completes. The delta calculation would be the End Time \- Start Time \= Execution Time (MS). 

 ***ii.***	    Testing Procedure: Test Functions

| ![][image7] |
| ----- |
| Figure 7: ‘[Images of Test Functions](https://drive.google.com/file/d/18_sUjBiaC14ooyrE4ud_xJRUxrT4d69J/view?usp=sharing)’ |

| ![][image8] |
| ----- |
| Figure 8: ‘[Images of Test Functions](https://drive.google.com/file/d/17u-fwV82oVIHUm9wGipQjXZRtAYalTIs/view?usp=sharing)’ |

Both implementations perform identical operations. The simple arithmetic increments a variable by a set amount (IncrementAmountBPCPP). The isolated logic has no external dependencies or I/O operations, and the pure calculation is focused solely on execution speed. 

 ***iii.***	    Testing Procedure: Mass Execution Testing

When we press the V key, we execute *n* sequential calls to each function; all *n* execution times are stored in an array. We get an average calculation using the mean value computed for a representative performance metric, and tests are repeated 10 times for statistical validity.

 ***iv.***	    Results and Analysis: Graph Interpretation

| ![][image9] |
| ----- |
| Figure 9: ‘[Image of the Graph conducted using Test Function Performance](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jPPQyT8thPkNEMbTokBaxVgRJVw7WtyH/view?usp=sharing)’ |

The blue line is BP which demonstrates exponential performance. The red line shows CPP which shows consistent, minimal execution time across all iteration counts. There was a drop between *n* \= 50,000 and *n* \= 60,000 for BP representing a failure to complete at 50,000. BP has shown instability even before the failure point, with inconsistent ability to complete all ten tests. 

 ***v.***	    Results and Analysis: Findings

There is a microsecond-level difference, as at low iterations (10,000-60,000), CPP was only hundredths of milliseconds faster; the exponential BP overhead, as BP execution time increased disproportionately with iteration count; the failure threshold, as BP cannot handle our required max calc operations (60,000+ iterations); and a real-world impact, as our tuning/learning calculation requires the performance profile CPP provides.

 ***vi.***	    Results and Analysis: Testing Biases & Control // Conclusion

Each loop completion included a print statement, affecting absolute times but not relative comparison. 10 tests were repeated with averaging to minimize random variance. All tests were performed on the same system to eliminate hardware variables. This test directly mirrors Vespa Mode’s actual requirements, as we ran functions every frame (60+ times/second), and even small frame differences were compounded significantly. Systems must handle increasing vehicle counts without degradation. This experiment gave us conclusive proof that BPs are sufficient for simple, infrequent operations and CPP is essential for performance-critical systems in Vespa mode. The BP failure at 50,000 iterations validates the refactoring decision by Vespa Mode, as our actual max calc requirements would be catastrophic for the performance of BP implementation. The hundredths of a millisecond difference at 10,000 iterations becomes much more of a problem at 60,000 iterations due to BP’s failure to complete all calculations, making CPP a requirement in Vespa Mode’s core system.
